paras: The lynching of Harrison Spencer was the abduction and killing of a Black farmer and local politician near Longview, Gregg County, Texas, in late August 1888 by a masked band that took him from his home at night. His body was found several days later hanging from a tree on Harris Creek, shot, whipped and mutilated. Papers tied the killing to his break with the Union Labor party, and the case was read into a United States Senate debate as an example of political murder in Texas.

Spencer, a farmer described as "a colored politician of note," lived on the A. S. Taylor place about a mile from Longview. A Longview special in the Austin Weekly Statesman called the county's three-way campaign among Democrats, Republicans and the Union Labor party very bitter and noted that a Black Democratic physician, Silas Sherman, had been warned by letter to leave. Spencer had recently left the Union Labor party; the earliest dispatches said he had declared for "the Democracy," the main wire for the Republican presidential and Democratic state tickets, and the New-York Tribune for the Republican ticket.

According to his wife, the only witness, Spencer went outside at night after hearing a noise, thinking stock had broken into the garden. She then heard voices like those of more than a dozen men and saw him forced onto an animal and carried off in his night clothes. Horse tracks were followed to the river at daylight, and the first reports supposed he had been drowned.

Deputy Sheriff Walter Reynolds later found the body about three and a half miles from Longview on the west bank of Harris Creek, and more than 100 citizens, white and Black, went to the scene. Spencer was hanging from a limb about fifteen feet up, hands tied behind him, with bullet wounds behind the left ear and in the left side; the correspondent judged he was shot before being hanged. The fuller wire text added whipping scars, advanced decomposition and a secluded spot with no public road nearby.

That afternoon County Judge J. T. Smith, Sheriff A. A. Killingsworth and County Attorney E. B. Bagland called "all law-abiding citizens" to the court house so that the perpetrators might be discovered, and 225 citizens answered. Governor Ross, at local request, offered $200 for each principal and accomplice, a Longview telegram reasoning from three sets of horse tracks that there were at least three. Gregg County offered $500, and citizens were expected to add more than $1,000, bringing the total above $2,000. No report of an inquest, arrest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage, and no suspect was named.

Texas and Southern reports blamed Black political rivals: the Statesman's Longview correspondent had "no doubt" Spencer was killed by men of his own color, blamed "malcontent office seekers and ignorant negroes," and predicted a lynching if the guilty were found. The Beatrice Daily Express blamed his "former colored political associates," and the Atlanta Constitution headed its report "Negro Kuklux Kill a Negro."

Northern headlines read the motive in opposite ways: the New York Evening World asked, "Was He Murdered for Being a Democrat?", while the New-York Tribune ran "Murdered for Being a Republican," omitting the attackers' supposed race and the Democratic tickets. The Daily Kennebec Journal reprinted the Tribune text, the Emporia Weekly News ran the wire as "Killed by Klu Klux," and the Maysville Evening Bulletin as "The Penalty of Political Desertion." In a Senate debate reported in October, Senator Chandler of New Hampshire read the Tribune account in reply to Senator Reagan of Texas as "the killing of a Republican because he was a Republican."

Accounts differed on the attackers: the Texas specials and the main wire version said the band was "supposed" to be made up mainly of Black men, while the Tribune and the Senate debate presented it as a Ku Klux band without stating race. They also differed on dates: the abduction is placed on "last Saturday" (August 25), August 27 or August 28, and the discovery is datelined August 30 or August 31.

reader.title: Lynching of Harrison Spencer
bases: A masked band took Spencer from his home at night and he was found shot, whipped and hanging from a tree (A4, A6, A10).

Spencer was killed and hanged by a masked band, of over a dozen men by his wife's account and at least three by the horse tracks (A4, A11, A6); the papers give a partisan motive, punishment for leaving the Union Labor party, rather than an accusation of crime, so the pretext element is uncertain (A7, A6).

A Longview special in the Austin Weekly Statesman, the Tribune's Longview special, the general wire and San Antonio state news independently agree on the abduction and the hanged, shot body (A4, A6, A10, A5).

framing.detail: The Austin Weekly Statesman's Longview correspondent called Spencer of 'the best character' but blamed 'malcontent office seekers and ignorant negroes' and predicted a lynching of the guilty.
The Atlanta Constitution headed it 'Negro Kuklux Kill a Negro'; Maysville 'The Penalty of Political Desertion'.
The New-York Tribune headed it 'Murdered for Being a Republican' and 'A Ku Klux Outrage'; Sen. Chandler used it as proof of political murder in Texas.
The San Antonio Daily Light called the murder 'entirely uncalled for'.
Emporia ('Killed by Klu Klux'), Kennebec and Philipsburg carried wire or reprinted texts.
